text: Here's something strange about London.
All over the city, there are these little green huts.
They look like garden sheds.
But if you walk in and try to sit down, someone will politely ask you to leave.
Unless you drive a black cab.
To understand why, we have to go back to a freezing night in 1875.
say: To understand why, we have to go back to a freezing night in eighteen_seventy-five.

text: Back then, London's taxis were pulled by horses.
And the drivers sat outside, high up on the back, in the wind and the snow.
That night, a newspaper man called George Armstrong needed a ride home.
He walked outside, and the street was full of taxis.
Horses, cabs, everything.
But not one driver.
Every single one of them was in the pub.
You see, the rule was simple. If your taxi was parked on the stand, you had to stay with it.
You couldn't just walk away and leave your horse.
So on a freezing night, a driver had two choices.
He could sit on top of his cab and freeze.
Or he could pay someone to watch his horse, and go somewhere warm.
And the warmest place on any street was the pub.
So most of them went to the pub.
Which isn't great when your job is driving.
Armstrong had an idea.
What if the drivers had their own warm room, right next to their taxis?
So he teamed up with some rich friends, and they started building huts.
The very first one went up near his own house, in St John's Wood.
Inside, there was hot food and hot tea.
A man worked inside, selling food to the drivers.
And there were three rules.
No drinking. No gambling. And no swearing.
But there was a problem.
The huts had to sit right on the road, next to the taxis.
And on a London road, nothing could be bigger than a horse and cart.
So that's exactly how big they made them.
Not one inch bigger.
Inside, about ten to thirteen drivers squeezed around one long, thin table.
And it worked.
Over the next forty years, they built 61 of them all over London.
say: Over the next forty years, they built sixty-one of them all over London.

text: Most are gone now.
But 13 are still standing, and every single one is a protected building.
say: But thirteen are still standing, and every single one is a protected building.

text: They're still run by the same charity, and they still feed drivers today.
So if you're in London and you see a little green hut, you now know what it is.
You can even buy a sandwich at the window.
Just don't try to sit down inside.
That seat is only for the drivers.
